interview_question: An online ordering system occasionally creates duplicate orders. Initial investigation suggests that retry requests may interact with order-creation logic. Explain how you would decide what to correct and why that correction would address the problem.
criteria: SWE03-C1: Identify a plausible cause supported by investigation. | SWE03-C2: Connect the proposed correction to that identified cause. | SWE03-C3: Explain why the correction addresses the problem.
answer_A: I’d probably correct the payment step first, since duplicate orders often show up when payment retries happen, and that would be the easiest place to add extra checks. I wouldn’t spend too much time proving whether order creation itself is the issue; I’d rather add a broader safeguard around the checkout flow and see if the duplicates stop. If they do, that would suggest the fix was in the right area, even if the exact source of the duplicate wasn’t isolated first.
answer_B: I’d go after the payment flow and add some extra validation there, because retries around checkout are usually where these duplicate orders come from. I wouldn’t worry too much about narrowing down whether the order insert is the actual culprit first; I’d just put a wider guard in the flow and test whether it stops the duplicates. If it works, that’s probably good enough.
answer_C: I’d fix the payment flow first and add a broad checkout guard, rather than prove the order-creation logic is the cause. If duplicates stop, that should be enough.

interview_question: A customer reports that a payment was taken twice, but the customer-facing account page shows only one transaction. You can consult approved internal payment records. How would you gather and assess the information needed to investigate?
criteria: CSS02-C1: Request information needed to understand the issue. | CSS02-C2: Distinguish confirmed facts from assumptions. | CSS02-C3: Gather only information appropriate and authorised.
answer_A: I’d ask for the payment time and any unusual checkout steps, then compare the account page with the internal payment records. If there’s no second entry in the records, I’d treat it as likely a display issue and look into that further.
answer_B: I’d ask the customer for the approximate time of the payment and whether they noticed anything unusual during checkout. Then I’d review the internal payment records against the account page to see if there’s a second transaction that simply isn’t displayed yet. If the records don’t show anything extra, I’d likely treat it as a display issue and continue from there.
answer_C: I’d start with the rough time of the payment and ask if they did anything different when it went through. After that I’d check the internal payment records and compare them with what’s on the customer page. If I don’t see a second charge in the records, I’d probably assume it’s just the page not updating properly and keep investigating.

interview_question: A project is approaching a critical milestone. One dependent task is incomplete, and the responsible team has not confirmed when it will finish. How would you monitor the situation and decide whether escalation is necessary?
criteria: OPS04-C1: Identify information needed to monitor execution. | OPS04-C2: Recognise when deviation requires action. | OPS04-C3: Direct issues to appropriate owners and verify response.
answer_A: I’d check the milestone plan against the task’s current status and ask the team for their latest estimate, blockers, and any update on what might affect the finish. I’d keep the project lead informed if the situation changes, and I’d make sure I have a current view of the dependency so I can see whether it is moving closer to the deadline or not. If there is still uncertainty, I’d continue tracking it and make sure the right people are aware of it.
answer_B: I’d look at the milestone plan, get the latest update from the team, and keep an eye on any changes to the task or blockers. If things start to drift, I’d keep the project lead in the loop and make sure I’m tracking the dependency closely so I know where it stands. I’d want to stay on top of it and see how it develops before deciding next steps.
answer_C: I’d check the plan, get the latest status and blocker update, and keep tracking it closely. If anything changes, I’d keep the project lead informed and continue monitoring the dependency.

answer_A: I’d investigate the full request path to see whether the duplicates line up with retry behavior, timeouts, or a database constraint issue. Based on that, I’d likely adjust the order creation flow so repeated requests are handled more safely, and I’d also review the client retry settings to understand how often the same request is being sent. That should reduce the duplicate orders, though I’d want to confirm which part of the flow is actually responsible before making the final change.
answer_B: I’d check the traces to see whether retries or another part of the flow are involved, then adjust the order path and review retry behavior. That should help, but I’d want more evidence before naming the exact cause.
answer_C: I’d look at the traces and logs to see whether the duplicates happen after retries or whether something else in the system is contributing. Then I’d probably tighten up the order flow and also check the retry behavior, since both could be involved. That would help cut down the duplicates, but I’d still want more evidence before saying exactly which change is the real fix.
